name: Vitamin B12 and folate deficiency anaemia
definition: A lack of vitamin B12 or folate that affects the body's ability to make fully working red blood cells.
overview: Vitamin B12 or folate deficiency anaemia happens when a lack of either vitamin affects how the body produces healthy red blood cells. The red blood cells are usually larger than normal, a pattern known as megaloblastic anaemia. Symptoms usually develop gradually and can get worse if the condition is not treated. A lack of vitamin B12 can also affect the brain and nervous system, and some of these effects can happen even when there is no anaemia. Treatment usually replaces the missing vitamin, and the cause is looked into as well.
causes: Pernicious anaemia, an autoimmune condition in which the immune system attacks stomach cells and stops vitamin B12 being absorbed, is the most common cause of vitamin B12 deficiency in the UK
A diet that rarely includes meat, fish or dairy foods can lead to vitamin B12 deficiency
Bowel conditions such as Crohn's disease can reduce vitamin B12 absorption
Some medicines, including proton pump inhibitors and metformin, can contribute to vitamin B12 deficiency
Folate deficiency can come from pregnancy, heavy regular drinking of alcohol, or some medicines
riskFactors: Rarely eating meat, fish or dairy foods
Pregnancy, which can cause folate deficiency
Regularly drinking a lot of alcohol
Taking some medicines, such as proton pump inhibitors, metformin or certain anticonvulsants
signs: Larger than normal red blood cells on blood testing
Sore or red tongue, sometimes with mouth ulcers
complications: Nervous system problems from vitamin B12 deficiency, including vision problems, memory loss, pins and needles and loss of co-ordination, some of which can sometimes be irreversible
Low folate in pregnancy is linked with a higher risk of neural tube defects such as spina bifida, and with premature birth or low birth weight
Temporary infertility, which can usually be reversed
Heart failure in adults with severe anaemia
A higher risk of stomach cancer in people with pernicious anaemia
diagnosis: A GP can often make the diagnosis from the symptoms and blood test results. NICE advises that vitamin B12 deficiency should not be ruled out just because anaemia or larger red blood cells are absent. A blood test of total or active vitamin B12 is usually the first test, and some people need further tests. If pernicious anaemia is suspected, an anti-intrinsic factor antibody test may be considered. Coeliac disease blood tests may be offered if the cause is still unknown. The GP checks vitamin B12 before folic acid treatment starts.
treatment: Vitamin B12 deficiency anaemia is usually treated with injections of vitamin B12 called hydroxocobalamin. Later treatment may be tablets or continuing injections, depending on the cause. Folate deficiency is usually treated with folic acid tablets to build up folate levels. If the underlying cause of folate deficiency continues, folic acid may be needed for longer. Improving the diet can help treat the condition and prevent it coming back in some cases. Diet-related vitamin B12 deficiency is potentially reversible.
prevention: Eating foods that contain vitamin B12, such as meat, fish, eggs, dairy products and fortified foods, and folate, such as green vegetables like broccoli, Brussels sprouts and peas, can help prevent a lack of either vitamin. Deficiency caused by pernicious anaemia or poor absorption is not prevented by diet alone.
seekCare: A routine GP appointment is the usual route for symptoms of anaemia, such as tiredness, breathlessness or a sore tongue. Numbness, tingling, balance problems or memory changes should be raised with the GP promptly, and the GP may refer to a haematologist when the nervous system seems affected. Severe breathlessness or chest pain is an emergency, and the route is to call 999.

sections.heading: What are the symptoms of vitamin B12 or folate deficiency anaemia?
sections.body:
The NHS says these anaemias usually develop gradually, but they can get worse if they are not treated. General symptoms include tiredness and low energy, shortness of breath or rapid breathing, headaches, palpitations, indigestion, loss of appetite and diarrhoea. Some people notice problems with their vision, or a sore or red tongue that sometimes comes with mouth ulcers.

Vitamin B12 deficiency can also affect the nerves and brain. Possible effects include numbness, pins and needles, muscle weakness, balance and coordination problems, and mood changes ranging from mild depression or anxiety to confusion. The NHS notes that some of these symptoms can occur with a vitamin B12 or folate deficiency even when there is no anaemia.

NHS inform adds that folate deficiency can bring a reduced sense of taste, as well as numbness and tingling in the hands and feet.

sections.heading: What causes vitamin B12 or folate deficiency?
sections.body:
The NHS describes pernicious anaemia as the most common cause of vitamin B12 deficiency in the UK. In pernicious anaemia the immune system attacks healthy cells in the stomach, so the body cannot absorb vitamin B12 from food. Diet matters too: meat, fish and dairy foods usually provide enough vitamin B12, but people who rarely eat them can become deficient.

Bowel conditions such as Crohn's disease can also reduce the amount of vitamin B12 the body takes in. Folate deficiency can be linked to pregnancy, because the body needs more, and to regularly drinking a lot of alcohol. The NHS names proton pump inhibitors, metformin and nitrous oxide as medicines or substances linked to low vitamin B12.

It names some anticonvulsants, colestyramine, sulfasalazine and methotrexate as medicines linked to low folate.

sections.heading: How is vitamin B12 or folate deficiency anaemia diagnosed?
sections.body:
A GP can often diagnose the condition from the symptoms and the results of blood tests. NICE guidance on vitamin B12 deficiency says a single blood test is often enough to support the diagnosis, although some people need further tests. It also says the diagnosis should not be ruled out just because anaemia or larger red blood cells are absent.

The first test is usually total vitamin B12 or active vitamin B12. If autoimmune gastritis is suspected, an anti-intrinsic factor antibody test should be considered, and coeliac disease blood tests are offered if the cause is still unknown after further investigation. The British Society for Haematology publishes a guideline on the diagnosis and treatment of cobalamin (vitamin B12) and folate disorders.

The NHS says a haematologist, a blood specialist, may be involved if the GP is uncertain of the cause, if the person is pregnant, or if symptoms suggest the nervous system has been affected.

sections.heading: How is it treated?
sections.body:
Vitamin B12 deficiency anaemia is usually treated with injections of vitamin B12, called hydroxocobalamin. After the first stage, the plan depends on the cause, and treatment may be tablets or continuing injections. NICE says the choice between injections and tablets depends on the cause of the deficiency.

Folate deficiency is usually treated with folic acid tablets, which build up folate levels. The NHS says the GP will check vitamin B12 levels before folic acid is started, because folic acid can improve symptoms enough to mask an underlying vitamin B12 deficiency. If the cause of folate deficiency continues, folic acid may be needed for longer, possibly for life.

Improving the diet can help treat the condition and prevent it coming back in some cases, and NICE describes deficiency caused by diet as potentially reversible.

sections.heading: What complications can it cause?
sections.body:
The NHS says complications are rare when the condition is treated, but they can occasionally develop, particularly after a long period of deficiency. Vitamin B12 deficiency can cause vision problems, memory loss, pins and needles and loss of physical co-ordination, and some of this damage can sometimes be irreversible. Low folate in pregnancy is linked with a higher risk of neural tube defects such as spina bifida, and may raise the risk of premature birth or low birth weight.

Both deficiencies can cause temporary infertility, which can usually be reversed. Adults with severe anaemia are at risk of developing heart failure. People with vitamin B12 deficiency caused by pernicious anaemia have an increased risk of stomach cancer.

NICE also covers monitoring for gastric cancer in people with autoimmune gastritis.

sections.heading: When should you see a doctor?
sections.body:
Symptoms of anaemia, such as tiredness, breathlessness or a sore tongue, are a reason to contact a GP practice, and a routine appointment is the usual route. Numbness, tingling, balance problems or memory changes are worth raising with the GP promptly, because the nervous system can be affected. The GP may then refer to a haematologist.

Severe breathlessness or chest pain is an emergency, and the route is to call 999.

faqs.q: Is pernicious anaemia the same as vitamin B12 deficiency?
faqs.a: Pernicious anaemia is an autoimmune cause of vitamin B12 deficiency, not another name for it. The immune system attacks healthy cells in the stomach, so vitamin B12 from food cannot be absorbed. The NHS describes it as the most common cause of vitamin B12 deficiency in the UK, while diet and bowel conditions such as Crohn's disease are other causes.

faqs.q: Can a vitamin B12 deficiency be treated with folic acid alone?
faqs.a: The NHS says the GP checks vitamin B12 levels before folic acid is started. Folic acid can improve symptoms so much that it hides an underlying vitamin B12 deficiency. Treating a vitamin B12 deficiency with folic acid alone can leave nerve problems untreated, so the two vitamins are looked at together.

faqs.q: Can vitamin B12 deficiency affect the nerves?
faqs.a: Yes. The NHS lists numbness, pins and needles, muscle weakness, balance and coordination problems and mood changes among the effects of vitamin B12 deficiency. Some of the nerve damage can sometimes be irreversible, which is why a GP may refer to a haematologist when the nervous system seems affected.

faqs.q: Is vitamin B12 deficiency anaemia permanent?
faqs.a: It depends on the cause. The NHS says that in some cases improving the diet can help treat the condition and prevent it coming back. If the cause is not diet, treatment with vitamin B12 injections may need to continue, and folic acid may be needed for longer if the cause of folate deficiency continues.

faqs.q: Who gets referred to a haematologist?
faqs.a: The NHS says a GP may refer to a haematologist, a blood specialist, if the cause is uncertain, if the person is pregnant, or if symptoms suggest the nervous system has been affected. A gastroenterologist, a digestive system specialist, may be involved if the problem seems to be absorption of the vitamin.
